'''Indigenous statistics''' is a quantitative research method specific to [[Indigenous people]].<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology">{{Cite book |last1=Walter |first1=Maggie |url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.4324/9781315426570/indigenous-statistics-maggie-walter-chris-andersen |title=A Quantitative Research Methodology |last2=Andersen |first2=Chris |publisher=Routledge |year=2016 |isbn=9781315426570 |doi=10.4324/9781315426570}}</ref> It can be better understood as an Indigenous quantitative methodology. Indigenous quantitative methodologies include practices, processes, and research that are done through an Indigenous lens.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" />

The purpose of indigenous statistics is to diminish the disparities and inequalities faced by Indigenous people globally.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Statistics are a reliable source of data, which can be used in the present and future.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research">{{Cite book |last1=Mertens |first1=Donna M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4omBQ_SVShMC&dq=indigenous+pathways+into+social+research&pg=PA5 |title=Indigenous Pathways Into Social Research: Voices of a New Generation |last2=Cram |first2=Fiona |last3=Chilisa |first3=Bagele |date=2013-04-15 |publisher=Left Coast Press |isbn=978-1-59874-696-9 |language=en}}</ref> This is a relatively new concept in the research world.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Statistics are the collection of quantitative data that is used to interpret and present data.<ref name="Britannica">{{Cite web |title=Statistics {{!}} Definition, Types, & Importance {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/science/statistics |access-date=2022-12-09 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref> Indigenous refers to an ethnic group of people who are the earliest inhabitants or native to that land.<ref name=":dictionary.com">{{Cite web |title=Definition of indigenous {{!}} Dictionary.com |url=https://www.dictionary.com/browse/indigenous |access-date=2022-12-09 |website=www.dictionary.com |language=en}}</ref> Connecting these two terms, researchers aim to provide fair and reliable data on Indigenous communities.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /><ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> By focusing on three central themes, which are situated in entering research through a solely Indigenous lens. The cultural framework of data, quantitative methodologies in data, and the situated activity amongst academic research.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" />               

== Background ==

=== Statistics ===
[[Statistics]] are a collection of quantitative data.<ref name="Statistics">{{Cite web |title=Definition of STATISTICS |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/statistics |access-date=2022-12-09 |website=www.merriam-webster.com |language=en}}</ref> Statistics are how data is interpreted and presented.<ref name="Britannica" /> Statistics interpret our reality and influence the understanding of societies.<ref name="Britannica" /> The purpose of Indigenous statistics is to have Indigenous people collect their own data in a fashion they find best suitable for their community.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /><ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> This is done by Indigenous researchers, or through the perspective of Indigenous communities.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /> Statistics, in turn, provide information used to determine theoretical and practical development and produce the notion of open data.<ref name="Britannica" /> Indigenous statistics aims to make statistics a source of reliable information regarding Indigenous societies.   

=== Indigenous people ===
[[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous Peoples]] is a term used to define people with ancestral origins in the land they inhabit. Indigenous peoples are the earliest known inhabitants of the land they inhabit.<ref name=":dictionary.com" />  

== Concerns with open data ==
[[Open data]] is making statistics available to the public.<ref name="Data">{{cite journal |last1=Kitchin |first1=Rob |title=The Data Revolution: Big Data, Data Infrastructures & Their Consequences |journal=SAGE Research Methods |date=2014 |doi=10.4135/9781473909472 |publisher=SAGE Publications Ltd}}</ref> The data should be easily accessible, and this is often done through a [[web portal]].<ref name="Data" /> Scholars have criticized the way open data is collected today.<ref name="Data" /> For instance, some have said that open data is not politically or economically benign.<ref name="Data" /> Others have made critiques regarding elements of open data that are not as honest as they first appear, thereby affecting certain people differently.<ref name="Data" /> The key concern is whether or not these initiatives bring forth value, impact, transparency, participation and foster economic development.<ref name="Data" /> Many of the critiques of open data are not to abandon the movement but to find more sustainable ways that are equitable and transparent for all.<ref name="Data" /> For example, open data has not always been the fairest to Indigenous populations. Open data may lead to data being used to perform misleading and prejudicial work or put non-Indigenous services managing Indigenous relations that misrepresent them due to cultural assumptions.<ref name="Data" /> Indigenous people are also not accounted for in state datasets. They are restrained from informing their impacts and are not able to rely on this data for solutions.<ref name="Data" /> Indigenous statistics, push to remove these barriers and minimize the risk of misrepresentation and misinformation being published on [[indigenous people]].<ref name="Data" />

== Theoretical framework ==
Indigenous statistics is a relatively new concept, recently gaining attraction in the research world.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> It aims to decolonize the data and provide fair statistics to Indigenous communities.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /><ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Indigenous statistics critique the production of open data and conclusions being drawn from open data statistics.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /><ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> ''Indigenous Statistics'' is the first book to be published on quantitative Indigenous methodologies.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> It was written by authors Maggie Walter and Chris Andersen.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> It was published on September 15, 2013, by [[Taylor & Francis|Routledge Taylor & Francis Group]].<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> ''Indigenous Statistics'' offer a new lens in researching statistics, by critiquing the ways in which quantitative data have framed Indigenous people, and offers new forms of quantitative data to better represent the Indigenous populations.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> The authors focus on three main topics. They first investigate the cultural framework of Indigenous statistics, how methodologies, not methods produce Indigenous statistics and how academic research is a situated activity.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" />

=== Cultural framework ===
The cultural framework within Indigenous statistics is one that focuses on the collection, analysis, and interpretation of statistics about Indigenous people.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Indigenous scholars claim that the representation of Indigenous people in statistics actually is a representation that reflects the dominant nation-state rather than the subjects being analyzed.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> The objective here is to focus on the ways in which statistics produced by the nation-state may push and drive certain narratives about Indigenous people that may not be a true representation.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Indigenous statistics call for their own empowerment and control to produce and collect data according to their societies' own needs.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Approaching research through an Indigenous lens, is not one of the strict or clear-cut guidelines.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /> Taking an Indigenous research approach will look different based on the need of the research.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /> An initiative that took an Indigenous approach when conducting the cultural framework of their research is, The Te Atawhai o Te Ao Institute, which is based in [[Whanganui|Whanganui, New Zealand]].<ref name="kainga">{{Cite web |title=Kāinga |url=https://teatawhai.maori.nz/ |access-date=2022-12-09 |website=Te Atawhai o Te Ao - Independent Maori Institute for Environment & Health |language=en-NZ}}</ref><ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /> This institute is dedicated to Indigenous based research that will generate and rediscover knowledge focused on health and the environment for the benefit of [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous people]].<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /><ref name="kainga" />   

=== Indigenous quantitative methodology ===
Indigenous quantitative methodologies are methodologies in which the practices and processes are taken from an Indigenous standpoint.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> This means that all aspects of the research and methodologies are influenced by an Indigenous lens.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" />

Standpoints influenced by an Indigenous lens; Indigenous Social Position, Indigenous Epistemology, Indigenous Ontology, Indigenous Axiology.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" />

The methodologies of collection, interpretation, and analysis produce statistics rather than the research method itself.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> The focus is on the motives and reasoning behind certain research, more than what type of research is being conducted to find the information.<ref name="Indigenous pathways into research" /><ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> [[Methodology]] is a central understanding of Indigenous statistics as it helps provide context for many steps of the research.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Methodologies help determine why and how research questions are asked instead of other questions.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> How, when, and where the data was collected and how the data was interpreted and used.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Methodologies are important because they provide the user with insights from how the data was collected and governance over it, to the personal identity of the researcher and understanding of their objectives.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" />

One way the census' can further improve on methodologies on Indigenous statistics is through [[Statistics Canada]]'s "ethnic mobility" category.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Canada recognizes Indigenous people into three categories, First Nations, Metis, and Inuit.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> These categories today are meant to be inclusive diverse representations of all Indigenous people, yet is the categories the Canadian government attempt to govern the diversity of Indigenous people, rather than reflecting the actual diversity amongst these communities.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> For example, the term First Nation captures the image of dozens of different tribal societies sharing some similarities, but the Canadian Government recognizes them as one people entirely.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> 

=== Academic research ===
Indigenous statistics' sole purpose is to provide equitable and transparent data on Indigenous people that is fair and honest to them.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> The focus on Academic research being a situated activity, is to draw attention to how research may mislead or misrepresent the statistics being presented.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Academic research either helps push the truth out or as in the past, be used to push specific narratives. Throughout history, there have been institutions that recorded and published qualitative data.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" /> Academic research is situated within the dominant society of their nation-state, and the development of Indigenous statistics into the research world, looks to remove these systemic barriers and begin finding more equitable and fairways of conducting and publishing research on Indigenous groups.<ref name="A Quantitative Research Methodology" />
